mcqs.question: A single shared gateway has accumulated a growing pile of "if mobile, trim these fields; if web, include these extra ones" conditional logic. What pattern addresses this specific problem?
options: Backend-for-frontend (BFF) — give each client type its own dedicated gateway tuned to its needs
Removing the gateway entirely and having every client call backend services directly
Adding a service mesh, since that's the fix for any gateway complexity
Rate limiting more aggressively to reduce the number of requests needing this logic
mcqs.explanation: The BFF pattern exists exactly for this: splitting a single overloaded gateway by client type lets each one evolve independently without accumulating client-specific conditionals in one shared codebase. Removing the gateway loses its centralized auth/rate-limiting value; a service mesh addresses internal service-to-service traffic, not this client-facing shaping problem; rate limiting doesn't touch the conditional-logic issue at all.

mcqs.question: A team wants mTLS and automatic retries between their own internal microservices, with no involvement from the external-facing entry point. What's the right tool for this?
options: A service mesh — it operates on east-west, service-to-service traffic inside the system
The API gateway, since it's the single place all traffic should be controlled from
A backend-for-frontend, since it's designed for internal traffic patterns
This isn't achievable without merging all services into a single deployable
mcqs.explanation: The compare slide draws this line explicitly: a gateway handles north-south traffic (external clients in), while a service mesh handles east-west traffic between internal services, including exactly these concerns — mTLS, retries, circuit breaking. A gateway isn't positioned for internal service-to-service traffic, a BFF is about client-type variation not internal mesh concerns, and merging services isn't required to get mTLS/retries.

mcqs.question: A team adds a pricing discount rule directly into the gateway's routing logic because "the gateway already sees every request anyway." What's the risk the pitfall slide describes?
options: There's no meaningful risk since the gateway is a natural place for any logic that touches every request
The gateway becomes a shared bottleneck — every domain team now has to coordinate through the same central codebase, and one team's bug can break routing for everyone
The only risk is slightly slower response times, with no structural downside
This is fine as long as the discount logic is well-tested in isolation
mcqs.explanation: Domain-specific business logic belongs with the team that owns that domain; piling it into the shared gateway creates a central bottleneck where unrelated teams must coordinate deploys, and a bug in one team's pricing logic can take down routing for every other service behind the same gateway. This is a structural coupling risk, not just a performance concern, and good test coverage of the logic itself doesn't remove the coupling problem.
